summary: Help 7–9 year-olds understand that meteorologists are scientists who predict weather by combining data from many instruments (satellites, radar, weather balloons) and computer models, and that forecasts carry uncertainty (rain is often given as a percentage chance) rather than being certainties, while still helping people plan and stay safe. Teach forecasting as a chain: gather data → spot the pattern/incoming system → predict → people act. The central activity is a predict-then-check forecasting role so children can feel both the VALUE of a forecast and the reality of uncertainty; alternatives include a tool-reveal studio, an expert interview, and fact-check matching.
misconceptions: Forecasters just guess / look out the window — they combine data from many instruments and models
A forecast is a certainty, so a 'wrong' forecast means forecasters failed — forecasts are probabilities
Radar and satellite are the same thing — they gather different information
The forecast controls the weather rather than predicting it
Longer-range forecasts are just as reliable as tomorrow's — uncertainty grows with time

activities.title: Be the forecaster: predict, then check
steps: Take in the day's evidence for your town: a satellite view showing cloud sweeping in, radar lighting up with rain, and a weather balloon's upper-air reading.
Describe what the data shows together—e.g. 'a rain system is approaching from the west'—and say which tool told you what.
Issue tomorrow's forecast as a symbol plus a chance, e.g. 'rain, 80% chance.'
Watch townspeople who trusted the forecast act—grabbing umbrellas or cancelling a sailing trip—then advance time to reveal the actual weather.
Run several days. On a day you forecast '80% rain' but it stays dry, discuss: was the forecast a failure, or was a dry day one of the less-likely outcomes?
Finish by forecasting from your own class weather diary: predict tomorrow from your recorded pattern, then check it the next day.
activities.insight: A forecast is not one person guessing or looking out the window—it is reading many instruments and models to predict a likely outcome, stated as a probability, so people can make real decisions. A forecast can miss without the forecaster having failed.

activities.title: Forecasting studio: meet the tools and their jobs
steps: Explore a forecast studio where each tool can be revealed in turn: satellite, radar, weather balloon, computer model.
For each tool, state its distinct job in your own words: satellites see cloud from above, radar tracks where rain is, balloons sample the upper air, computers model the weather forward.
Arrange the tools into the forecasting pipeline: tools → data → pattern → forecast → people prepare.
activities.insight: Different instruments gather different information, and a forecast is built by combining them—radar and satellite are not the same thing.

activities.title: Interview a meteorologist
steps: Ask a meteorologist (in role) open questions: How do you make a forecast? Which tools do you trust most, and for what? Tell me about a time a forecast kept people safe. Why are you sometimes wrong?
Answer the meteorologist's questions back, such as 'Given this incoming cloud and rising rain on the radar, what would you predict?'
Afterwards, write one sentence defining what a meteorologist is and one reason their work is useful for safety or daily planning.
activities.insight: A meteorologist is a scientist who studies and predicts weather from data, and their forecasts help people make safe, practical decisions—while always carrying some uncertainty, so they can sometimes miss.

activities.title: Fact-check: tools, jobs and why forecasts help
steps: Match each tool to the job it does (satellite→see cloud from above; radar→track rain; balloon→sample upper air; computer→model weather forward).
Answer short questions on why forecasting is useful (e.g. choose the real decision a forecast could change) and on what a probability like '70% chance' means.
Explain in a sentence why a forecast for a week from now is usually less reliable than tomorrow's.
activities.insight: Secure the factual core: which tool does what, why forecasts matter, and that a percentage is a chance, not a promise.

checkQuestion: The forecast said '70% chance of rain tomorrow,' but the next day stayed dry. Was the forecast wrong? And how does a meteorologist come up with a forecast in the first place?
checkAnswer: Not necessarily wrong — a 70% chance means rain is likely but not certain, so a dry day is one of the possible outcomes. Meteorologists forecast by collecting current weather data (instruments, satellites), spotting patterns and how weather systems move, and running models to predict. They PREDICT the weather, they don't control it, and forecasts are probabilities that get less certain further ahead.
